extracted.intended_audience: investigative journalists, journalism researchers, journalism students, and practitioners involved in cross-border data-driven investigations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for organizing, conducting, and judging investigative data-journalism projects (especially large, cross-border collaborations such as ICIJ Panama/Paradise Papers). Emphasizes methods, ethics, division of labor, coordination, and risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes of investigative reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative reporting can be characterized by three main attributes: (1) it comprises original work that (2) reveals concealed information that is (3) of public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three attributes as a core test for whether a project qualifies as investigative reporting; prioritize public interest when balancing other concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labor — by story vs by task
rubrics_metrics.description: Teams typically divide work either (1) by stories (e.g., people/businesses/countries/regions) or (2) by (technical) tasks (e.g., research, writing, editing, fact-checking, infographics, video, podcast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a division model that fits team size and skills; expect team sizes to vary (2–30 people) and frequently grow during investigations. Explicitly assign roles for data processing, story finding, verification, and publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core task — digging up stories
rubrics_metrics.description: A central task is 'digging up stories': gathering and running lists of people through systems, working with the structured part of the data, and finding and structuring other small parts of the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose lists of target names (political/economic elites, celebrities) and leverage international collaborators for local expertise. Emphasize careful, repeated checking to avoid homonyms and misidentification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data handling and structuring
rubrics_metrics.description: Make leaked/large datasets accessible and structured for investigation: run lists, match dates of birth, managers’ positions, ownership, and convert unstructured portions into usable structured datasets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement multiple independent checks (e.g., 'Three other colleagues checked every name I had provided'); use external databases and registries to corroborate; track provenance and transformations of data to prevent errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and corroboration with external sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Find proof beyond the leaked data by confronting data findings with local financial and business information and by obtaining statements from implicated people and experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on leaked documents; conduct interviews, seek expert interpretation, compare with land records and public registries, and ensure findings can be independently corroborated before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead investigator / coordinator responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead investigators coordinate the whole investigation process, maintain contact with project partners and central organizations (e.g., ICIJ headquarters), oversee research, interviews, story production, and act as liaison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads should document decisions, maintain communication channels, and balance hands-on investigation with coordination to ensure consistency and prevent duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central coordination and network roles
rubrics_metrics.description: A central organization or headquarters (e.g., ICIJ) often provides coordination, infrastructure, and key contact persons who facilitate exchange, support, and collaborative writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the benefits of central coordination (infrastructure, synchronization) and the attendant power/knowledge asymmetries; plan for transparent decision-making where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical prohibition — do not alter quotes or photographs
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents are unanimous in strict rejection of altering quotes and photographs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Altering primary materials is unacceptable and undermines credibility; never fabricate or manipulate quoted material or images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical prohibition — do not accept money from sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists reject accepting money from sources; payment-for-information is widely disapproved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid financial relationships with sources that create conflicts of interest or imply personal enrichment; disclose any borderline cases to editors and consider refusing the material if payment was involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical prohibition — do not publish unverified content
rubrics_metrics.description: There is unanimous rejection of publishing unverified content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require rigorous fact-checking and verification before publication; unverified leaks should not be made public without corroboration and editorial oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditionally acceptable covert methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Some methods meet with partial approval under certain circumstances: using personal documents (letters, pictures) without permission; gaining employment at an organization to obtain inside information; using hidden microphones or cameras.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat covert methods as ethically sensitive and justify them internally; weigh public interest and necessity, legal risk, and potential harm; seek editorial/legal clearance and limit use to cases where there is no less-invasive alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversial use of unauthorized confidential documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Using confidential business or government documents without authorization is controversial — acceptable to some only under certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess importance to public interest, authenticity, and legal exposure; consult lawyers and editors and document provenance and chain of custody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversial sharing with NGOs or third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving information to NGOs or external actors is controversial among respondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit sharing outside of journalistic collaboration networks; consider confidentiality obligations, source protection, and editorial independence before sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling leaks and anonymous sources — credibility and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaked information should be used if it is credible and relevant, but it must be rigorously checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize verification of leaked data, trace authenticity, and corroborate with independent sources; treat relevance to public interest as a key filter for use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling leaks and anonymous sources — anonymity and knowledge of source
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources’ wishes for anonymity are widely accepted, though most respondents still prefer that the source is at least known to the journalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect anonymity when necessary for safety, but where possible obtain background knowledge of source motives and credibility; if identity is unknown, increase verification efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling leaks and anonymous sources — consider source motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must account for sources’ possible agendas and motivations when assessing the information provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate potential motivations and selection biases in leaked materials; treat motives as one factor in assessing use and framing, but prioritize authenticity and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest as a deciding principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Public interest is a leading principle against which source anonymity and other considerations must be weighed; some journalists will use information even if the source has 'bad' intentions if the disclosure is of public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use public-interest justification carefully and document reasons for publication decisions; balance public benefit against potential harms to individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy and embargo rules in collaborative projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Strict secrecy rules (e.g., ICIJ’s rules) can prevent journalists from approaching experts or confronting subjects until coordinated release, causing uncertainty about story viability until near publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan verification and expert consultation within secrecy constraints; establish internal protocols for secure expert consultation and for timed releases to manage editorial risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication strategy and outlet availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding a medium to publish can be a major challenge; journalists may need to change outlets or publish in foreign media if their home outlet will not run the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop publication plans early, including contingency outlets and timing; consider legal, editorial, and safety implications of chosen outlets and jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time pressure, staging of data releases, and late entry
rubrics_metrics.description: Deadlines and staggered uploads can create intense time pressure; journalists joining late may need to work long hours to catch up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate phased data releases, allocate resources for peak work periods, and maintain clear task lists and priorities to manage late-stage workloads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination across teams and editorial cultures
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperating with journalists from other newsrooms requires keeping track of who is working on what, maintaining communication, and negotiating differing values and cultures about approach and timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up shared tracking tools, regular briefings, and agreed protocols for approaches to subjects and publication timing; surface and mediate editorial conflicts early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding and using expert sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations often require credible experts willing to spend days examining documents and to agree to embargoes; such experts are necessary to interpret complex financial schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit trusted experts, offer appropriate confidentiality arrangements, and budget time for expert review; corroborate experts' claims and disclose expert affiliations as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource constraints — finance, staff, time
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of financial resources, staff, and time is a frequent obstacle to comprehensive investigative reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan budgets, seek collaborative funding or partner organizations, prioritize high-impact leads, and use networked collaboration to pool scarce resources and expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to information and legal threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-transparent governments, lack of freedom-of-information laws, and threats of legal action (libel suits, prosecution, raids) hinder investigations and can endanger journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess legal environment early, consult legal counsel, consider cross-border publication strategies, maintain secure data handling, and prepare for legal defense and safety measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threats, harassment, and personal safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists face threats ranging from legal pressure and advertising withdrawal to violence, death threats, and smear campaigns; threats affect journalists even in countries with formal press freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize source and journalist safety: use secure communications, protect identities, prepare risk mitigation plans, and coordinate with central organizations for legal and security support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust, shared norms, and selection into networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborative investigative projects depend on trust and shared professional norms; organizations often require nomination/appointment and have opaque selection processes, which affects network composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster shared ethical guidelines, onboarding processes, and transparent criteria where possible; ensure collaborators understand and agree to common verification, secrecy, and publication rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of networked collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Large international collaborations increase capacity to find relevant stories, share skills and knowledge, and mitigate some risks by dispersing knowledge across many hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage complementary national expertise and technical skills; use distributed teams to cross-check findings and to ensure that information is not concentrated in a single vulnerable location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power asymmetries and opacity in centralized networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Central individuals and headquarters can hold superior knowledge and coordination power; democratic structures (e.g., board appointments) may be opaque and selection criteria unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of information and power asymmetries; document decisions and lines of authority to reduce resentment and ensure fair access to project information where feasible.
